conversation.content: Let's design a Twitter-like feed system. Users post tweets, follow other users, and see a timeline of tweets from people they follow. What questions do you have?

Yeah so — I actually built something like this at my last company, feed system for 20M users. So the thing is, the fan-out question is like the core of everything here, right? Like do we do fan-out-on-write or fan-out-on-read, and it depends on — well first, how many users? And follower distribution matters a lot because celebrities just wreck — anyway, what's the scale?
300M DAU, average user follows 200 people. Some accounts have 50M+ followers. Let's go with that. Can you walk me through the high-level architecture in an organized way?

Right so the architecture — well actually the first thing I want to talk about is the fan-out because that's where we had all our problems. So fan-out-on-write means when a user tweets, you immediately push that tweet ID into every follower's timeline cache. Redis sorted sets work great here, we used them, scored by timestamp. The problem is — wait, let me back up. The high-level components are: tweet write service, timeline service, fan-out service, and a social graph service. And the user service obviously. Plus the feed ranking but — okay so the tweet comes in, hits the write service, persists to the database, then the fan-out service takes over. For normal users with like 500 followers, fan-out-on-write is fine. But for someone with 50 million followers — we actually had this exact issue — you can't push to 50 million timelines synchronously. Takes forever and the memory is—
Let me stop you there. You're mixing the high-level architecture with the fan-out deep dive. Can you first just lay out the components and the request flow cleanly? Then we'll dive into fan-out.

Sorry, yeah. Okay. So: User posts a tweet. It goes through an API gateway to the Tweet Write Service, which persists it to a tweets table — probably sharded MySQL or Postgres by user_id. Then the Fan-out Service is notified asynchronously via a message queue. The Fan-out Service looks up the poster's followers from the Social Graph Service and distributes the tweet to followers' timelines. For reading, the Timeline Service retrieves a user's precomputed timeline from a Redis cache. If the cache is empty or expired, it falls back to assembling the timeline on the fly from the tweets table. That's the basic flow.
Good, that's much clearer. Now let's dive into the fan-out problem you were eager to discuss. How do you handle the celebrity case?

So this is where it gets really interesting because we tried three different approaches at my company before we got it right. The answer is a hybrid model. You set a follower threshold — we used 10,000 but Twitter apparently uses something higher, maybe 100K — and accounts above that threshold use fan-out-on-read instead of fan-out-on-write. So when a celebrity tweets, you don't push to 50 million timelines. You just store the tweet. When a user loads their timeline, the Timeline Service pulls their precomputed feed from Redis (which has all the normal-user tweets fanned out), then also queries the latest tweets from any celebrity accounts they follow, merges them in real time, and returns the combined feed. The merge is fast because each user follows maybe 5-10 celebrities. It's a small number of point reads. At my old company — sorry, tangent, but we actually had a bug where the threshold was misconfigured and a marketing account with 2 million followers got fan-out-on-write treatment and it—
I appreciate the experience but let's stay focused. The hybrid model is right. Tell me about the Redis memory management for the timeline cache — how much memory do you need?

So this is where most people get the math wrong. Each user's timeline is a Redis sorted set of tweet IDs. You don't store the tweet content in every timeline — just the IDs. A tweet ID is 8 bytes, the score (timestamp) is 8 bytes, sorted set overhead per entry is about 40 bytes. So roughly 56 bytes per entry. If we keep the last 800 tweets per timeline, that's about 45KB per user. 300M DAU times 45KB is 13.5TB. In practice not all 300M users are actively loading their feed, so maybe you only keep hot timelines — say 100M users with active timelines — that's 4.5TB. Across a Redis cluster with 64GB instances, you need about 70 nodes. We used 128GB instances and had — well anyway, 70 nodes is manageable.
Excellent memory analysis. That's the kind of depth I was looking for. Now, what's the eviction strategy when a user hasn't loaded their feed in a while?

Right so — there's actually two levels of this. First, the sorted set itself: we cap it at 800 entries and use ZREMRANGEBYRANK to trim the oldest entries whenever we add new ones. That keeps each timeline bounded. Second, for users who haven't logged in — like if someone hasn't opened the app in 2 weeks — we don't want their timeline sitting in Redis eating memory. We'd use a TTL on the sorted set key, maybe 7 days. When they come back, their timeline key is gone, so the Timeline Service has to reconstruct it. We query the social graph for their followees, pull recent tweets from each, merge and sort, populate Redis, and return. That reconstruction is expensive — it's fan-out-on-read — but it only happens once and then we're back to fan-out-on-write for subsequent tweets. The cold start latency is maybe 200-500ms for that first load. At my last job we had a whole incident around this where — actually never mind, the point is the TTL-based approach works.
Good. Let's talk about the database design. How do you store tweets and the social graph?

Tweets table — sharded by user_id so you can quickly fetch all tweets by a user. Columns: tweet_id, user_id, content, created_at, media_urls, reply_to_id. The social graph — so this is where it gets tricky because you need both directions. Who does user A follow, and who follows user A. We had this adjacency list in MySQL sharded by — hmm, actually the problem is if you shard by follower_id, looking up 'who follows user X' requires a scatter-gather across all shards. And if you shard by followee_id, looking up 'who does user X follow' requires scatter-gather. So you kind of need both. We stored it twice — one table sharded by follower_id, one by followee_id. Denormalized. Writes go to both. It's a classic — oh, and for the fan-out service, it needs the followers list, so it reads from the followee-sharded table. The timeline reconstruction reads from the follower-sharded table. Each query is single-shard.
That's a great insight on dual-sharding the social graph. Let's discuss the API design briefly.

So POST /tweets for creating, GET /feed for timeline, GET /users/{id}/tweets for a user's tweets. The feed endpoint needs cursor-based pagination — not offset-based because the feed is constantly changing. The cursor is the last tweet ID the client saw. Oh and — I always forget to mention this — the feed endpoint should support both 'latest' and 'ranked' modes. Ranked mode applies an ML ranking model on top of the chronological feed. We'd have a lightweight ranker that reorders the top N candidates. But actually the ranking piece is a whole separate system, maybe we shouldn't—
Right, let's skip ranking. Talk to me about failure scenarios. What happens if the Fan-out Service goes down?

So the Fan-out Service sits behind a message queue — Kafka, in our case — so if the service goes down, messages queue up in Kafka. When it comes back, it processes the backlog. Tweets are still persisted in the database by the Write Service, so nothing is lost. Timelines just get stale temporarily — users see slightly outdated feeds until the backlog is cleared. The key thing we learned is you need to monitor the consumer lag. If the fan-out consumers fall behind by more than, I don't know, 5 minutes, you alert because timelines are getting noticeably stale. We had a time where — sorry, the point is: Kafka decouples write availability from fan-out availability. Tweets still post fine even if fan-out is lagging.
Good. What about a Redis cluster failure? Not a single node, but a full cluster outage.

If the entire Redis cluster goes down — okay so first, that shouldn't happen because you have replicas and — but hypothetically. All timeline reads now have to be reconstructed on-the-fly from the database. For 300M DAU that's a disaster. Each timeline read becomes a fan-out-on-read: query the social graph, fetch recent tweets from 200 followees, merge. That's 200 database reads per feed request. Even with batching, at the traffic volume you'd melt the database tier. So you need — this is exactly what happened to us once. We had a partial Redis outage and the database got hammered. The solution is circuit breakers and degraded mode. If Redis is down, serve a limited feed — maybe just the user's own tweets and tweets from their top 10 most-interacted-with accounts. And you bring Redis back with — sorry I keep going off on tangents. The main thing is you need a fallback that doesn't require reading 200 users' tweets per request.

That's a practical answer clearly informed by real experience. Let me ask about a different dimension: how do you handle a tweet that goes viral? Someone with 500 followers posts something that gets retweeted to reach 100 million people.

So this is different from the celebrity problem because the original poster is a normal user. The viral spread happens through retweets. Each retweet is itself a tweet from the retweeter, so the fan-out for each retweet goes through the normal fan-out path. If a user with 10M followers retweets it, that single retweet triggers the celebrity fan-out path — fan-out-on-read. The original tweet content is fetched from the database and it becomes a hot key. That's where you need — hmm, there's like three things happening at once. The hot tweet object in the database gets hammered with reads. You cache it. The retweet counter needs to update. You batch those counter updates — don't write to the DB on every retweet, buffer in memory or Redis and flush periodically. And the fan-out from all the retweeters is — well it's just normal fan-out happening in parallel across many retweeters, each going through the appropriate write or read path based on their follower count.
You mentioned the tweet becoming a hot key in the database. How specifically do you handle that? Redis caching alone might not be enough if the cache node holding that key is overwhelmed.

Right — single key on a single Redis node, everyone requesting it. The standard trick is to replicate the hot key across multiple Redis nodes. You append a random suffix — like tweet:{id}:shard_0 through tweet:{id}:shard_9 — and the client randomly picks one. Spreads the read load across 10 nodes instead of 1. We did this at my old job and — oh also you can use local in-process caches on the application servers. A 5-second TTL local cache means most requests never even hit Redis. For a viral tweet the content doesn't change, just the counters, so the cache is highly effective.
Good techniques. Let me ask one more thing. How do you handle deleting a tweet? A user deletes something that's already been fanned out to millions of timelines.

Tweet deletion is — okay so there's the database side and the cache side. Database: you soft-delete the tweet, mark it as deleted. For the Redis timelines, you have a choice. You could fan out the delete the same way you fan out the write — push a delete operation to every follower's timeline. But that's expensive and for a celebrity with 50M followers, it's the same problem as the write fan-out. Instead, you handle it lazily. When the Timeline Service assembles a feed response, it hydrates the tweet IDs from cache into full tweet objects. If a tweet ID resolves to a deleted tweet, you just filter it out at read time. The timeline cache still has the stale ID but it's harmless. Eventually it gets trimmed when new tweets push it out of the 800-entry window. It's eventually consistent but — yeah, that's how you'd do it. Lazy deletion at read time.
Can you give me a quick capacity estimate? How many fan-out operations per second does the system need to handle?

So — if we have, uh, 300M DAU and each posts maybe 2 tweets per day, that's 600M tweets per day. That's about 7,000 tweets per second. Average followers per normal user is... let's say 200 after removing celebrities from the fan-out. So 7,000 times 200 is 1.4 million fan-out writes per second to Redis. Each write is a ZADD to a sorted set, which is O(log N) — fast. Across a Redis cluster, 1.4 million writes/sec is doable with maybe 20-30 nodes dedicated to timeline writes. Though in practice you'd batch the fan-out — instead of individual ZADDs, pipeline them. We batched in groups of — honestly I don't remember the exact number, but batching cut our Redis load by like 80% because pipeline amortizes the round trip.

Alright, let's wrap up. You clearly have deep hands-on experience with feed systems — your knowledge of Redis memory management, the hybrid fan-out model, and hot key handling was impressive. However, your communication was a significant challenge throughout. You frequently jumped between topics, started tangents, and had to be redirected repeatedly. In a senior role, structured communication is critical, especially when presenting designs to stakeholders or mentoring others. The knowledge is there, but it needs to be delivered more clearly. Thanks for your time.

strengths: Deep practical knowledge of hybrid fan-out model — clearly informed by real production experience, including the celebrity threshold approach
Excellent Redis memory analysis — correctly calculated per-entry overhead, timeline sizes, and cluster sizing with specific numbers
Strong failure handling grounded in experience — Redis outage answer included degraded feed mode and circuit breakers from real incidents
Great hot key mitigation techniques — key replication with random suffix and local in-process caching
Insightful database design — dual-sharded social graph for bidirectional lookups is a sophisticated approach
weaknesses: Severely disorganized communication — jumped between topics constantly, started multiple tangents, abandoned sentences mid-thought
Required frequent interviewer redirects to stay on topic — at least 4 explicit redirections needed
War stories disrupted flow — repeatedly started anecdotes that didn't reach a conclusion before being cut off
Requirements gathering was brief and unstructured — jumped immediately into fan-out discussion
API design was an afterthought — cursory treatment of endpoints and pagination
